title: The Platform Sutra
hook: the teachings of Huineng, the sixth patriarch, as his students remembered them

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of the Xinxin Ming: faith and mind are not two. Your line: not two. When did the moment split into want and have, and did you say it? Day one thousand two hundred sixteen.

A young man is selling firewood in a market town in the far south of China. He's poor. The sutra says his father died when he was small, and he and his mother live on what the wood brings in. He delivers a bundle to a customer's lodging, and on his way out he hears a man inside reciting a sutra, the Diamond Sutra. He stops. Something in him opens at the words. He asks where the man learned it, and the answer is a monastery to the north, where a teacher named Hongren teaches. The young man's name is Huineng. Today: the book that tells his story.
screen: `FIREWOOD IN A SOUTHERN MARKET.` → `A SUTRA THROUGH A DOORWAY.` → `A TEACHER TO THE NORTH.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. The Platform Sutra presents itself as Huineng's own talks, given from a teaching seat, a raised platform, at a temple, and written down by his students. It opens with him telling his life, starting with the firewood. Second, the first meeting. Huineng arrives at Hongren's monastery and asks to become a Buddha. Hongren tests him: you're from the south, a barbarian, he says, using a rough word for southern people. How could you become a Buddha? Huineng answers: people may be northern or southern, but Buddha-nature has no north or south. Hongren hears it, says nothing more for the moment, and sends him to the back to split wood and pound rice. Third, two verses on a wall. Hongren asks his monks to write a verse showing what they've understood. The senior monk, Shenxiu, writes, in paraphrase: the body is the tree of awakening, the mind a bright mirror on its stand; wipe it again and again, and let no dust settle. Huineng can't read or write, the sutra says, so he asks someone to put his verse up beside it. In one widely retold version: awakening has no tree, the mirror has no stand; from the beginning there is not one thing, so where would dust settle? Fourth, what follows. Hongren calls him in secret, teaches him at night, and names him his heir, and so tradition calls Huineng the sixth patriarch. The rest of the Platform Sutra is his teaching, and we'll spend the coming days inside it.
screen: `TALKS FROM A TEACHING SEAT.` · `NO NORTH OR SOUTH IN BUDDHA-NATURE.` · `TWO VERSES ON A WALL.` · `HONGREN'S HEIR.` · then, large: `THE SIXTH PATRIARCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Huineng's story begins with the plainest line he could give: a poor boy, a widowed mother, a load of firewood. Sit with that for a moment. Let the breath settle. Then let the first plain line of your own story come up, the way you'd tell it if you weren't trying to impress anyone. Don't polish it. Just hear it once, and let it go. Then rest in the breath, nobody in particular, carrying no bundle at all. The bell holds the time.
The Platform Sutra. The teachings of Huineng, told from a teaching seat and remembered by his students, opening with his own story. Today's word.
Your line: the sixth patriarch. Today, when someone is sized up by where they come from, remember the woodcutter's answer: Buddha-nature has no north or south. Day one thousand two hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: In Zen and Chan communities the Platform Sutra is studied, and the story of Huineng's arrival and the two verses on the wall is retold in talks.

original.note: Chinese (Liuzu Tanjing): 'the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch'.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Platform Sutra is a sutra the Buddha taught on a platform.
what it means: the talks of Huineng, the sixth patriarch, given from a teaching seat and remembered by his students.
what a scholar hears: the verses on the wall differ between versions of the sutra; some readers note that the line 'from the beginning there is not one thing' belongs to one widely retold version.

notes: All paraphrased; no public-domain translation on the approved list. Nothing quoted.

Versions differ (Dunhuang vs. later Zongbao text). Huineng's verse 'from the beginning there is not one thing' is from the later, widely retold version; the Dunhuang text reads differently. The trapdoor says so; Keeper to confirm the wording.

Check: father died when he was young; sold firewood to support his mother; heard the Diamond Sutra recited at a customer's lodging; Hongren's 'barbarian' (獦獠) remark and Huineng's reply; work in the threshing room; illiteracy; secret night teaching and naming as heir.
